newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief expected to return to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief expected to return to Zaire.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila left his headquarters in southeastern Zaire on Thursday but a senior rebel official said he would return later the same day.
Rebel officials earlier said Kabila left Lubumbashi to visit some neighbouring countries before a first face-to-face meeting with President Mobutu Sese Seko, rescheduled on Thursday for Saturday.
But hours later, a senior official in Kabila's office said: "There are some important developments and the president is returning home tonight after consultations with neighbouring countries.
"Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha will hold a news conference later on Thursday to shed light on the developments," she said.
Kabila's original schedule was to visit neighbouring countries before flying to South Africa and the Saturday talks.

Rebel officials in Lubumbashi were initially unaware of the change to Saturday and said South African President Nelson Mandela, brokering the peace initiative as an African solution, would contact Kabila directly.

The rebel chief, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, told Reuters late on Wednesday his meeting with Mobutu would discuss the Zairean president's departure from power after 32 years.
"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," Kabila said.
As the talks were wrapped up, Kabila's forces advanced towards the town of Kenge on the way to the capital Kinshasa.
Kabila said Mobutu's army had begun blowing up bridges to try to slow the military push.
"They have started blowing up bridges in Kenge in order to stop our forces from advancing to Kinshasa. But that will not hinder us and if necessary we shall swim," Kabila said.
A mining expert who arrived in Lubumbashi from the area on Thursday told Reuters the rebels were advancing from the towns of Ilebo, Tshikapa, Kananga and Kikwit.

The expert, who declined to be named, said rebels from Ilebo and Kananga were advancing on foot while those from Tshikapa and Kikwit were using tanks and armoured personnel carriers and had long-range artillery pieces and bridge-laying equipment.

"It's big stuff. These guys are heavily equipped and should have no problems crossing the rivers in that area to Kenge and Kinshasa because they are equipped with bridge-laying gear and speedboats," he added.
The rebels have said they would enter Kinshasa within the next 10 to 15 days. The expert agreed: "From what I saw, that timescale makes a lot of sense. These guys are serious."
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson told reporters in Kinshasa on Wednesday there were no preconditions for the talks.

But in Lubumbashi, Kabila said he had not softened his position that Mobutu must agree to stand down. The rebel leader's aides said he had been surprised by Richardson's announcement in Kinshasa that "several African leaders" would attend the talks on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua.
The rebels do not want the talks to turn into a mini-summit about one of Africa's biggest political shake-ups for decades.
There was no indication Mobutu had agreed to step down.
In talks with Kabila on Tuesday, Richardson did not persuade him to accept a ceasefire ahead of the meeting or agree to accept a transitional government before elections.
"There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," Kabila said.
He launched his rebellion in Zaire last October. Rebels have made short shrift of Mobutu's ragged army and are poised to attack Kinshasa from Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) to the east.
